tagline: The otter that keeps the kelp forest standing
summary: The smallest marine mammal and the heaviest member of the weasel family, living along the rocky coasts and kelp forests of the North Pacific. With no blubber, it stays warm inside the densest fur of any animal, eats about a quarter of its body weight a day, and cracks shellfish open with stones.
ability: stone tools and the densest fur of any animal

stats.size: Males 1.2–1.5 m, females 1–1.4 m long; up to about 45 kg
stats.depth: Most foraging at 2–30 m; dives recorded to about 100 m
stats.range: Coastal North Pacific: the Kuril and Commander Islands, the Aleutians and Alaska to British Columbia and Washington, and central California
stats.diet: Sea urchins, crabs, clams, mussels, snails, abalone and other seabed invertebrates; some populations also eat fish

facts.title: Warm without blubber
facts.text: Unlike other marine mammals, sea otters have no blubber. They rely on the densest fur of any animal, with more than a million hairs per square inch at its thickest, which traps a layer of air next to the skin.

facts.title: Always hungry
facts.text: To keep its body at about 38 °C (100 °F) in cold water, a sea otter eats about a quarter of its body weight every day.

facts.title: Guardian of the kelp
facts.text: Comparing Aleutian islands with and without sea otters, Estes and Palmisano (1974) found that otters keep plant-eating invertebrates such as sea urchins in check. Where otters had been removed, grazing increased and kelp beds were destroyed.

facts.title: A rock in its pocket
facts.text: Sea otters break hard-shelled prey with stones, either holding the rock on the chest and pounding the prey against it or striking the prey with the rock. A loose fold of skin under each forearm can hold a favourite stone and food collected on a dive.

facts.title: Shallow feeders
facts.text: Sea otters fitted with depth recorders in south-east Alaska did most of their foraging between 2 and 30 m. Males often fed deeper than females, and the deepest foraging dives ranged from 35 to 100 m.

facts.title: Hunted to the brink
facts.text: Hunting for their fur in the 18th and 19th centuries greatly reduced the sea otter's range. Today three subspecies are recognised, and northern sea otters have been reintroduced to coasts from Alaska to Oregon.

notes: Taxonomy per WoRMS (AphiaID 242598). The IUCN page blocks scripted access; the 2021 assessment (Doroff, Burdin & Larson; assessed 21 January 2020, category Endangered A2abe) was confirmed through Crossref, the IUCN Otter Specialist Group's Red List document and the Monterey Bay Aquarium. The southern sea otter is separately listed as Threatened under the US Endangered Species Act. Depth: the 100 m maximum is the deepest foraging dive in Bodkin et al. (2004); the Monterey Bay Aquarium states that sea otters can dive to 600 ft (183 m), which could not be traced to a primary source and is not used for the gauge. Fur density: the aquarium gives more than a million hairs per square inch; ADW gives about 100,000 per cm² (about 645,000 per square inch), so 'densest of any animal' is used without a precise number in the summary. 'Smallest marine mammal' follows Yeates et al. (2007), cited in the deep chapters. 'Intelligent' shelf based on habitual stone-tool use. The Morro Bay photograph carries the photographer's credit line in the bottom-left corner; its Commons title says Piedras Blancas but the description places it at Morro Rock. The raft photograph's USFWS caption gives no location.
